title: Medellín (1968)
hook: Latin American bishops commit to the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, Populorum Progressio: development of every person and the whole person, and peace built by justice. Your line was development is peace. Did you follow through on your note? Day one thousand three hundred five.

A city in the mountains of Colombia, and a meeting room full of bishops from across Latin America. Outside, their continent: grand cathedrals, and not far from the cathedral steps, families with very little. The question on the table was simple to ask and hard to answer. What should the Church look like in a place like this? Rich and distant, or close enough to share the same street? The documents they wrote there are known by the city's name. Today's word is Medellín.
screen: `A CITY IN THE MOUNTAINS.` → `CATHEDRALS AND HUNGER.` → `WHAT SHOULD THE CHURCH LOOK LIKE?`

segments.voice: First, a text that sits close to their concern. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus reads from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Read beside Medellín, it sounds like a description of the Church's job, not only of Jesus's. Second, the word poverty, pulled apart. Their document on the poverty of the Church names three senses. There's poverty as lack: not enough food, housing, schooling. That, they say, is an evil, and not something God wants. There's spiritual poverty: an open, empty-handed trust in God, the poverty of the beatitudes. And there's poverty as a commitment: choosing, freely and out of love, to share the condition of the poor, to stand with them and work against what keeps them poor. Third, the turn toward themselves. The bishops asked their own Church to live more simply, to make its buildings, titles and ways of living plainer, and to be present where the poor are. Not a Church that hands things down to the poor from a height. A Church with the poor. Fourth, why it reaches past Latin America. Some readers trace the phrase from last week, the option for the poor, back to soil like this. Whatever the history, the shape is useful on any ordinary day: tell apart the poverty to fight, the poverty to welcome, and the poverty to choose.
screen: `ANOINTED TO PREACH TO THE POOR.` · `THREE KINDS OF POVERTY.` · `A CHURCH THAT LIVES SIMPLY.` · then, large: `NOT FOR THE POOR, BUT WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Latin America. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the map: Mexico down through Central America, the islands, the long sweep of South America to its tip. Let a few names come: a city, a country, someone you know with family there. Then let faces come, the street vendor, the grandmother raising grandchildren, the priest or nun working in a poor barrio. If you pray, you can hold that whole continent before God, and if you know a prayer in Spanish or Portuguese, you can use it. If you don't, simply wish them well, one place at a time. The bell holds the time.
Medellín. The Colombian city where Latin American bishops met and committed the Church to stand with the poor, and to become poorer itself. Today's word.
Your line: with the poor. Today, find one way to be alongside, not above: sit with someone, listen first, or ask before you help. Day one thousand three hundred five.

howItsDone: Many Catholic communities in Latin America and beyond draw on the Medellín documents in their work with the poor, through base communities, parish outreach and religious orders living in poor neighborhoods.

fork.setup: you're a bishop at Medellín. the cathedral is grand and the streets around it are poor. what do you commit to?
options: keep things as they are and send help from a distance.
a Church that lives simply and stands with the poor.
leave the question of poverty to governments.
fork.reveal: the bishops asked for a poorer Church, present among the poor, living out what Jesus reads in Luke 4:18: good news to the poor.

notes: The three senses of poverty (material lack as an evil; spiritual poverty; poverty as commitment) are paraphrased from the Medellín document 'Poverty of the Church' (§4). Confirm the summary and section numbering.
The call for the Church to live more simply and be present among the poor is paraphrased from the same document; confirm.
The link to the 'option for the poor' is put as 'some readers trace'; the phrase itself is not attributed to Medellín.
Luke 4:18 Douay-Rheims wording: confirm 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor'.
'Last week' refers back to day 1296 (the option for the poor).
Original is null: the Medellín documents were written in Spanish and no single word is clearly worth teaching.
Editor pass: no longer claims the Medellín bishops took Luke 4:18 as their charter (not verified in the document); the verse is now set beside Medellín by the script.
